strand_a.summary: These developments underline that addressing research career precarity and brain drain is more urgent than ever: research careers are not merely a workforce issue, but a strategic capability crucial to Europe’s competitiveness, resilience, prosperity, and technological leadership. ADVANCING RESEARCH CAREERS ACROSS EUROPE — Case study report 5. Since the publication of the CESAER 2024 report Research Careers: A Critical Choice for Europe, political momentum to attract and retain global research and innovation talent, both from within Europe and beyond, has intensified, exemplified by the launch of the Choose Europe for Science initiative—a measure that the Heitor report, CESAER, and other key stakeholders had already called for in 2024. Developments in 2025, including the launch of the Choose Europe initiative, further confirm the continued relevance of these recommendations: enhancing stability in research careers; achieving a better balance between temporary and permanent contracts; strengthening institutional support for early-career researchers; establishing the European Research and Innovation Careers Observatory; and further strengthening its evidence base with university-level data.

strand_a.title: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation
strand_a.summary: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation. Drawing on principles established in regulated industries—pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, aerospace and advanced manufacturing—the paper proposes that successful AI implementation depends on the same characteristics as successful technology transfer: reproducibility, robustness and validation; traceability and knowledge preservation; and process control and continuous verification. To put this view into practice, the paper introduces the AI Technology Transfer Framework (AITTF), a seven-stage governance model designed to help organisations transfer workflows, expertise and decision-making into AI-enabled systems while maintaining accountability, operational integrity and organisational memory.

strategic_pathways.reader_title: New MSCA pilot funds longer-term postdoctoral posts to counter research precarity
strategic_pathways.reader_what: A 22.5 million euro MSCA pilot selects institutions partly on the long-term job security they offer researchers.
strategic_pathways.reader_why: Ties EU research funding to employment conditions rather than project output alone.
strategic_pathways.reader_more: Choose Europe for Science is an MSCA pilot action aimed at making European research careers more attractive by tackling precarity and turning brain drain into brain gain. Academic and non-academic organisations recruit postdoctoral researchers with a view to employment beyond the project period, and its stated novelty is that applicants are assessed partly on the longer-term professional prospects they offer. A single legal entity in a Member State or Horizon Europe associated country applies, with associated partners possible. The call budget is 22.5 million euros, capped at 3.5 million per beneficiary, and projects should recruit at least three researchers for up to five years, with MSCA covering the first two to three. Full conditions sit in the 2025 MSCA Work Programme.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research infrastructures
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on research infrastructures. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of research infrastructures.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 3 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
3 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on research infrastructures for current or planned work.
A sudden security reclassification reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: The primary corpus contains 3 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Maintain alternative facilities and access routes for projects that depend on shared infrastructure.
Avoid a single access system becoming the only route into several European facilities.
Use common, targeted screening rules rather than broad restrictions that fragment European access.
watch_for: Research previously treated as open is moved into a more restricted security category.
Different European countries apply materially different access decisions to the same work.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Well supported enough to watch closely, with contextual signals reinforcing rather than carrying the case.

page_guarantee.rule: New records update candidate reasoning; the shelf is re-decided each scan from recomputed maturity. No record takes a slot automatically.
page_guarantee.creative_reserve: Reserve = grounded runners-up + a creative reserve of relevant, uncontradicted hypotheses (distant, cross-domain, emerging, weak-signal or partially grounded), at least 18 and topped up toward 45, rotated across wow levels with weight on surprise. They mature into page competition when grounded.

high_order_inference.publication_policy: Stage 7 claim-native selection treats the reasoning layer as a future-hypothesis corpus. Candidate formation is broad; missing roles, thin evidence and unrun counter-evidence tests lower maturity rather than forbidding the hypothesis. Grounded candidates compete only within their wow 1-5 bucket. Each product reserves three public slots per wow level (15 total), displayed 5-4-3-2-1 three times; surplus grounded findings remain reserve and weaker hypotheses remain developing.
high_order_inference.lifecycle_policy: Claim-native stock persists as page/reserve/developing tiers. Evidence is recomputed each scan; candidates can strengthen, weaken or move between tiers as new evidence arrives. Counter-evidence and falsifier results affect maturity and can kill a contradicted hypothesis, but an unrun challenge is not a ban on future-facing reasoning.
high_order_inference.candidate_search_policy: Missing-role and falsifier queries remain ordinary scanner discovery inputs and receive no admission waiver.

scenarios_2035.method: Two uncertainties define the frame: how many resources Europe has, and how strongly Europe is connected globally. The four worlds are scenarios, not forecasts. Each has four variants built from current shocks, risks and opportunities.

axes.horizontal: Less globally connected ↔ More globally connected

scenarios.name: Connected Growth
story: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.
Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “Governments are acting on research collaboration”; “Firms are raising large funding rounds”.
Not everything moved. “Advanced materials is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2026.” That was true in the 2020s and it is true now.
Someone read the signs early: “Joint public purchasing of AI compute could also be used to improve AI governance.” The bet worked.
The warning came early and was filed away: “€1 billion for research capacity, €22 million for recruiting researchers.” It is now the norm.
The trade-off is exposure: deeper global links also leave Europe more dependent on decisions, suppliers and disruptions outside Europe.

scenarios.name: Independent Scale
story: By 2035, strong European investment has built more research and technology capacity, but Europe works with a narrower set of global partners. Funding and infrastructure are strong, while security, resilience and European control shape who can take part.
It is the world where today's pull toward “Governments are acting on research capacity” wins out.
Some things never changed. In the 2020s the Radar noted: “Green technology is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2023.” In 2035 it still does.
One early bet paid off. The 2020s signal was “Both the EU and national governments are putting money into defence innovation.” In this world, it came true.
One risk quietly became routine: “Strategic autonomy is only as strong as industrial competitiveness.”
The trade-off is reach: Europe has more control, but fewer outside connections and less access to some global talent, markets and ideas.

story: Global links remain strong in 2035, but European research and innovation operate with tight resources. Ideas and people move easily, while many European teams depend on outside capital, infrastructure or partners to scale their work.
It grew out of two arguments the 2020s never resolved, until they were: “EU measures on access to Horizon Europe are multiplying” and “Restrictions on data centres are in force”.
A familiar pattern survived the decade: “Open science is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2020.”
One door that looked half-open in the 2020s swung wide: “US restrictions give Europe a chance to recruit researchers.”
And one warning was not heeded: “Research infrastructure is moving faster than its rules.” By 2035 it is simply how things work.
The trade-off is dependence: Europe stays connected, but often relies on others to finance, host or scale what it creates.

The trade-off is ambition: Europe reduces exposure, but has less capacity to build, experiment and compete at scale.

frames.title: Resources × Global connectedness
frames.question: Can Europe mobilise the resources it needs, and how connected is it to the world?
frames.method: Two uncertainties define the frame: how many resources Europe has, and how strongly Europe is connected globally. The four worlds are scenarios, not forecasts. Each has four variants built from current shocks, risks and opportunities.

scenarios.name: Connected Growth
story: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.
Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “Governments are acting on research collaboration”; “Firms are raising large funding rounds”.
Not everything moved. “Advanced materials is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2026.” That was true in the 2020s and it is true now.
Someone read the signs early: “Joint public purchasing of AI compute could also be used to improve AI governance.” The bet worked.
The warning came early and was filed away: “€1 billion for research capacity, €22 million for recruiting researchers.” It is now the norm.
The trade-off is exposure: deeper global links also leave Europe more dependent on decisions, suppliers and disruptions outside Europe.

scenarios.name: Independent Scale
story: By 2035, strong European investment has built more research and technology capacity, but Europe works with a narrower set of global partners. Funding and infrastructure are strong, while security, resilience and European control shape who can take part.
It is the world where today's pull toward “Governments are acting on research capacity” wins out.
Some things never changed. In the 2020s the Radar noted: “Green technology is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2023.” In 2035 it still does.
One early bet paid off. The 2020s signal was “Both the EU and national governments are putting money into defence innovation.” In this world, it came true.
One risk quietly became routine: “Strategic autonomy is only as strong as industrial competitiveness.”
The trade-off is reach: Europe has more control, but fewer outside connections and less access to some global talent, markets and ideas.

scenarios.name: Open Under Pressure
story: Global links remain strong in 2035, but European research and innovation operate with tight resources. Ideas and people move easily, while many European teams depend on outside capital, infrastructure or partners to scale their work.
It grew out of two arguments the 2020s never resolved, until they were: “EU measures on access to Horizon Europe are multiplying” and “Restrictions on data centres are in force”.
A familiar pattern survived the decade: “Open science is still on Europe's agenda, as it was in 2020.”
One door that looked half-open in the 2020s swung wide: “US restrictions give Europe a chance to recruit researchers.”
And one warning was not heeded: “Research infrastructure is moving faster than its rules.” By 2035 it is simply how things work.
The trade-off is dependence: Europe stays connected, but often relies on others to finance, host or scale what it creates.

scenarios.name: Constrained Europe
story: In 2035, Europe has fewer resources and weaker global connections. Governments and institutions protect a smaller core of capabilities, while new projects, partnerships and large investments become harder to sustain.
One of today's tugs of war settled here: “Studies find weak points: economies”.
Old habits held. Back then the Radar kept seeing “AI compute is being built country by country, not as one European effort.” It never went away.
The lucky break was visible years ahead: “European drone capability is starting to rely on new partnerships.”
Nobody acted on this 2020s red flag: “EU computing capacity is limited and geographically concentrated, with substantial dependence on non-European suppliers.” Now everyone lives with it.
The trade-off is ambition: Europe reduces exposure, but has less capacity to build, experiment and compete at scale.

support.source_statement: No single government level can address varied urban pollution sources; policy needs local evidence plus cross-level coordination.

support.title: Redirecting agricultural research spending could make productivity growth sustainable
support.source_statement: Emissions are projected to outgrow agricultural output globally, but reorienting high-income country research from yield maximisation towards input-saving technologies could cut chemical use by up to 30 percent with limited food price spillovers.

support.source: European Health and Digital Executive Agency
support.source_statement: The call's two topics carry indicative budgets of €125 million for industrial decarbonisation and €150 million for clean technologies.

support.title: Innovation capacity and sustainable outcomes do not always move together
support.source_statement: Member states form differentiated profiles, and strong innovation capacity does not automatically translate into stronger sustainability outcomes.

support.title: Applying transition governance principles across six European Green Deal policy domains

support.title: Corporate research units patent more green technology when the surrounding region already does
support.source_statement: Host-region green innovation intensity is significantly associated with both the occurrence and the count of green patents from resident corporate R&D units, indicating reverse technological spillovers from local context into corporate research, but only where the region is foreign, core, environmentally brown and more strictly regulated than the firm's home country.

support.title: Geopolitical risk and greener carmaking
support.source_statement: Higher geopolitical risk is associated with lower green productivity; AI, environmental policy and information access moderate the relationship.

support.title: How four European chip research centres pursue greener innovation, and what drives them
support.source_statement: A case study of four European RTOs with semiconductor cleanrooms found their sustainability-oriented innovation centres on cleanroom energy, water and exhaust optimisation and is driven chiefly by research funding and regulatory pressure.

support.title: Commission launches climate-resilience framework with research-to-market tools
support.source_statement: The Commission presents a new EU climate-resilience framework linking a proposed law, research-backed adaptation tools and innovation uptake.

The European Regulatory Mirage: Epistemic Dependence and the Limits of AI Governance. Abstract Over the last decade, the European Union has positioned itself as a global regulatory benchmark in digital governance through instruments such as the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This article argues, however, that European AI governance operates under a structural constraint: a gap between regulatory authority and the material and epistemic capacities required to enforce it.
